candidates.title: Google social login auto-links by email without anti-pre-hijacking: pre-registered account stays accessible to attacker after victim's Google login
candidates.description: SocialLoginQuery resolves the account purely by email__iexact and, for an existing user, issues a session and sets email_verified=True — but never invalidates the password the account already had. Registration does not require email verification, so an attacker can pre-register a victim's email with their own password (and their own unique phone). When the real mailbox owner later uses 'Login with Google', Google proves email ownership and the backend logs them into the ATTACKER-CREATED account — while the attacker's password remains fully usable. Both parties hold persistent sessions for the same account: the attacker retains silent read/write access to everything the victim does (profile PII, store claim now unblocked because email_verified is set True, billing data). The sibling buyer-side implementation (google_customer_login) documents and fixes exactly this threat as 'Anti-pre-hijacking' by calling set_unusable_password() and sealing tokens_valid_after; the platform-users domain never received the port.
candidates.root_cause: SocialLoginQuery (services/social.py:103-147) performs find-or-create by verified provider email but, on the existing-account branch, only fills email_verified/names — it does not check whether the matched account's email was ever verified, does not invalidate a usable password, and does not revoke outstanding sessions. The credential proof covers the EMAIL, not the party who chose the existing password.
candidates.intended_behavior: Mirror the customer-side contract (StoreApp/domains/customers/services/google.py:152-165): when Google proves ownership of an email that matches a pre-existing account, any usable password must be invalidated and prior sessions sealed, so only the mailbox owner (via Google or password-reset) retains access.

trace.description: user = User.objects.filter(email__iexact=email).first() — matches ANY account with that email, including one pre-registered by an attacker with unverified email and a usable password
existing-account branch sets profile.email_verified=True (and names) — no password invalidation, no session revocation, no check of prior verification state
_social_session_response -> RefreshToken.for_user(user) issues JWT+refresh cookie to the Google-verified caller while the pre-registrant's password still authenticates via /api/token/

candidates.evidence: services/social.py:85-164 (no hardening on existing-user branch) vs StoreApp/domains/customers/services/google.py:152-165 which explicitly comments 'Anti-pre-hijacking: Google probo la titularidad del EMAIL, no quien eligio la contrasena' and runs customer.set_unusable_password() + tokens_valid_after seal. AdminApp/domains/users/tests.py:638-650 codifies the unguarded auto-link. Registration (services.py:120-170) sets a usable password and does not require email verification.
candidates.conditions: Attacker pre-registers the victim's email via POST /api/register/ (needs one unique phone per account — phone_hash uniqueness limits scale to targeted attacks) before the victim's first Google login; victim then authenticates with Google on the same email.

execution.command: manage.py test AdminApp.domains.users.tests.SocialAuthTests (extend with pre-registered usable-password account)
payloads: POST /api/auth/google/ {credential: <victim's Google ID token for victim@gmail.com>}
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: social login returns 200 with session for victim AND password login still returns 200 for attacker on the same User row; profile.email_verified=True afterwards.

candidates.remediation: In SocialLoginQuery's existing-account branch, replicate the customer hardening: if user.has_usable_password() -> user.set_unusable_password() and blacklist all OutstandingToken for the user (reuse _revoke_sessions); keep email_verified/names fill. Optionally only auto-link when the account's email was already verified or the account was social-created.

severity.rationale: Requires targeted pre-registration of a specific victim email (phone uniqueness prevents mass farming), but yields durable shared access to the victim's account and PII until the victim performs a password reset — and the sibling code proves the threat model was known.

candidates.title: Google login issues fresh sessions for is_active=False (deactivated) platform users
candidates.description: The platform password path is gated by Django's authenticate() -> ModelBackend.user_can_authenticate, which rejects is_active=False. The Google path bypasses that entirely: SocialLoginQuery looks the user up by email and _social_session_response calls RefreshToken.for_user(user) with no is_active check anywhere. A staff-deactivated account (Django admin is the only deactivation surface found) can therefore obtain brand-new access+refresh sessions via POST /api/auth/google/ as long as the email matches a Google-verified account. The buyer-side auth explicitly re-checks customer.is_active after google_customer_login (auth_views.py:556-557); the platform side has no equivalent.
candidates.root_cause: Missing is_active gate on the federated session-issuance path: neither SocialLoginQuery (services/social.py:85-164) nor _social_session_response (views/auth_views.py:435-460) inspects user.is_active, unlike the password path which inherits the check from django.contrib.auth.authenticate.
candidates.intended_behavior: Any session-issuing path must reject deactivated principals identically to the password path (and to the customer domain's explicit post-login is_active check).

trace.description: User.objects.filter(email__iexact=email).first() returns the user regardless of is_active; no is_active check in the whole function
RefreshToken.for_user(user) mints refresh+access for the deactivated account; refresh rotation then keeps the session alive

candidates.evidence: services/social.py full read — zero is_active references; AdminApp grep shows no is_active check in users auth. Contrast: StoreApp/domains/customers/views/auth_views.py:269 and :556-557 return 403 'Esta cuenta esta inactiva' for deactivated customers on BOTH password and Google login.
candidates.conditions: A platform user is deactivated (is_active=False, e.g., via Django admin ban) and possesses a Google account whose verified email equals user.email.

execution.command: source review + optional: set user.is_active=False then POST /api/auth/google/ with mocked tokeninfo
payloads: POST /api/auth/google/ {credential: <Google ID token, email == deactivated user's email> }
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: 200 with access+refresh cookies; no code path consults is_active.

candidates.remediation: Add `if not user.is_active: raise SocialAuthError()` (or return 403) in SocialLoginQuery/_social_session_response; consider a JWTAuthentication/get_user is_active check or token blacklist on deactivation for parity with existing sessions.

severity.rationale: Ban/deactivation evasion requires staff action plus a matching Google identity; impact is full account access for a principal the operator believed disabled.

candidates.title: Email-verification token is not bound to the email address: a stale link verifies a newly changed, never-proven email
candidates.description: EmailVerificationTokenGenerator._make_hash_value signs only user.pk + user.password + timestamp + profile.email_verified — the email address is absent. UpdateUserQuery lets an authenticated user change user.email and resets email_verified=False, but a verification token issued before the change remains valid (all hash inputs unchanged while verified stays False). VerifyEmailQuery then sets email_verified=True on the account whose email is now an address whose owner never received any link. The flag is the anti-abuse gate for claiming a public store (stores viewset create, viewset.py:460), so the attestation 'this mailbox is ours' is forged.
candidates.root_cause: _make_hash_value (services/services.py:202-209) omits user.email from the signed material, so the token proves only 'this user requested verification at time T', not 'this specific address was proven'.
candidates.intended_behavior: email_verified must attest control of the CURRENT user.email; changing the address must invalidate outstanding verification tokens (include the email — or a hash of it — in the token value).

trace.description: UpdateUserQuery changes user.email and resets email_verified=False without invalidating previously issued tokens (verified was already False -> hash identical)
profile.email_verified==True unblocks store creation — now attesting an unproven address

candidates.evidence: services/services.py:179-209 (generator), :38-56 (email change resets flag only), :345-361 (verify marks flag). Attack sequence fully source-traceable: register own@email -> token T issued -> PATCH /api/user/ {email: victim@x.com} (UserUpdateSerializer, self-scoped) -> GET /api/verify-email/?uid&token=T -> email_verified=True for victim@x.com.
candidates.conditions: Attacker controls any registered account; changes email within the 24h token window (EmailVerificationTokenGenerator.timeout=86400).

execution.command: extend AdminApp.domains.users.tests with: make_token -> UpdateUserQuery(email change) -> check_token still True
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: check_token compares identical hash inputs -> token validates -> verified=True on the new address.

candidates.remediation: Include user.email (or its HMAC) in EmailVerificationTokenGenerator._make_hash_value so any email change invalidates outstanding links; alternatively bind verification to the address the mail was sent to.

severity.rationale: Trivially executable by any user but the payoff is limited to forging the verified-email attestation (store-claim gate; phone anchor still required) and misdirecting account mail to the victim address.

candidates.title: No Origin/Referer check on platform session-issuing endpoints -> login CSRF (session donation) on /api/token/ and /api/auth/google/
candidates.description: CustomTokenObtainPairView and GoogleAuthView plant the session cookies (davent_refresh httpOnly + davent_csrf) in the response with no validation of the request Origin/Referer and no pre-session anti-CSRF token. DRF APIViews are csrf_exempt, the endpoints accept application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies (a plain cross-site HTML form POST parses into request.data), and SameSite=Lax does not prevent a top-level navigation POST — the Set-Cookie on that first-party navigation response is stored. An attacker auto-submitting a form with THEIR credentials (password, or a Google credential minted with the public client_id from /api/config/) leaves the victim's browser holding the attacker's refresh+CSRF cookies; the SPA's silent refresh then logs the victim into the attacker's account, and everything the victim subsequently enters (billing PII, store content) is visible to the attacker. The buyer-side auth implements exactly this defense — _session_origin_allowed is invoked on register/login/google — but it was never ported to the platform auth views.
candidates.root_cause: Missing origin binding on cookie-session issuance: neither CustomTokenObtainPairView.post (auth_views.py:232) nor GoogleAuthView.post/_social_session_response (auth_views.py:435-460,529-538) checks Origin/Referer against the request host or trusted origins, unlike the sibling customer endpoints.
candidates.intended_behavior: Session-issuing endpoints must reject cross-site POSTs (Origin/Referer allowlist = request host + CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS + CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS), matching _session_origin_allowed semantics used for customer auth.

trace.description: post() performs lockout+auth and sets cookies — no Origin/Referer validation anywhere in the file
_set_refresh_cookie/_set_csrf_cookie store the attacker's session in the victim's browser; SPA refresh (frontend/src/api/http.js:147-185) then authenticates as the attacker

candidates.evidence: StoreApp/domains/customers/views/auth_views.py:114-144 defines _session_origin_allowed with comment 'Anti login-CSRF ... Set-Cookie aplica igual aunque SameSite=Lax' and calls it at :232,:260,:532. No equivalent exists under AdminApp/ (grep for Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch across repo .py files returns only the customer implementation).
candidates.conditions: Victim visits attacker page that auto-POSTs a form to the platform origin; victim then uses the SPA while unknowingly logged into the attacker's account.

execution.command: host a page with <form method=POST action='https://<platform>/api/token/'> auto-submitting attacker's username/password (+remember=true)
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: 200 + Set-Cookie davent_refresh/davent_csrf stored as first-party cookies on the navigation response; subsequent /api/token/refresh/ with X-CSRFToken succeeds -> victim session = attacker's account.

candidates.remediation: Port _session_origin_allowed (or equivalent Origin/Referer allowlist) into CustomTokenObtainPairView.post and GoogleAuthView.post before issuing cookies; apply the same check to any future session-issuing endpoint.

severity.rationale: Classic login CSRF: requires victim interaction and continued use of the site under the wrong identity; impact is exposure of data the victim enters into the attacker's account rather than direct account takeover.

candidates.title: AnonRateThrottle subclasses skip authenticated users -> authenticated attacker gets unbounded password-reset emails (mail bombing / SMTP+queue abuse)
candidates.description: Every auth-endpoint throttle in AdminApp/domains/users/views/auth_views.py subclasses plain rest_framework AnonRateThrottle (LoginRateThrottle, RefreshRateThrottle, PasswordResetRateThrottle, PasswordResetConfirmRateThrottle, SocialAuthRateThrottle, PublicConfigRateThrottle). DRF's AnonRateThrottle.get_cache_key returns None when request.user.is_authenticated — and JWTAuthentication populates request.user on every request regardless of the view's AllowAny permission. Any registered user (open registration) therefore bypasses ALL these IP buckets entirely. The highest-impact instance is PasswordResetRequestView: each POST /api/password-reset/ for an existing email enqueues send_password_reset_email -> a real SMTP send per request, with no per-user or per-email cap — unlimited mail-bombing of arbitrary victims through DAVENT's sender identity plus Celery/SMTP queue flooding that can delay transactional mail (invoices, verifications). The buyer-side code explicitly avoids AnonRateThrottle for exactly this reason ('NO se usa AnonRateThrottle porque saltaria la cuota a un comprador autenticado', customers auth_views.py:164-168) using a customer.pk-or-IP keyed throttle instead.
candidates.root_cause: Throttle classes chosen as AnonRateThrottle subclasses inherit the authenticated-skip semantics; no fallback per-user throttle exists on the AllowAny auth endpoints.
candidates.intended_behavior: Auth endpoints that emit side effects (emails, provider calls, token issuance) must be rate-limited for BOTH anonymous and authenticated principals — e.g., a SimpleRateThrottle keyed by user.pk when authenticated else IP, as the customer domain does.

trace.description: PasswordResetRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle): DRF get_cache_key returns None for request.user.is_authenticated -> allow_request always True for any valid-JWT caller
RequestPasswordResetQuery -> send_password_reset_email.delay -> SendPasswordResetEmailQuery sends one real email per accepted request, unbounded for authenticated callers

candidates.evidence: auth_views.py:115-153 (all throttle classes are AnonRateThrottle/UserRateThrottle subclasses; only logout/resend use UserRateThrottle which is correct for their IsAuthenticated/AllowAny mix but logout is AllowAny -> see hardening). Contrast StoreApp/domains/customers/views/auth_views.py:164-178 CustomerRateThrottle keyed by customer.pk or IP with explicit anti-AnonRateThrottle comment. settings.py:75-79 DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES are overridden by view-level throttle_classes.
candidates.conditions: Attacker holds any valid platform account (free registration) and a Bearer access token; target email must exist for the mail to send (enumeration is NOT possible — response stays generic).

execution.command: register one account, obtain access token, loop POST /api/password-reset/ {email: victim} with Authorization: Bearer <access>
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: throttle get_cache_key=None -> no 429 regardless of volume; each existing-email request enqueues an SMTP send.

candidates.remediation: Replace AnonRateThrottle subclasses on side-effect auth endpoints with a throttle keyed by user.pk when authenticated else IP (port CustomerRateThrottle pattern); add a per-target-email cap for password-reset requests.

severity.rationale: Trivially exploitable by any registrant but impact is bounded to email abuse/Sender-reputation and queue pressure — no data exposure or account compromise.

hardening: LogoutRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle) on AllowAny TokenLogoutView does NOT throttle anonymous requests (UserRateThrottle.get_cache_key returns None for anon) — the comment 'acotado por usuario o por IP si no hay auth' is inaccurate; impact is minor (blacklist needs a valid token) but the claim should be fixed or the scope changed to a SimpleRateThrottle keyed by IP.

Platform auth throttles are plain AnonRateThrottle/UserRateThrottle — they lack the _pinned_ident REMOTE_ADDR pinning and _ResilientThrottleMixin fail-open used by DaventProject.throttling and the customer CustomerRateThrottle; a Redis outage turns login/reset endpoints into 500s instead of degrading gracefully.

request.data.get('username') type-confusion: a JSON body with username as object/array/int reaches _login_fail_key's .strip() -> AttributeError -> 500 on POST /api/token/ (also via _register_login_failure on the 400 path). Robustness bug, no security bypass — coerce/validate type before use.

VerifyGoogleCredentialQuery (platform) omits the iss+exp double-checks that the sibling verify_google_credential applies (customers/services/google.py:92-99); tokeninfo already enforces both server-side so this is defense-in-depth only.

davent_remember cookie is unsigned client input: a caller can self-set it to extend refresh lifetime to 30d on each rotation — equivalent to the login-time remember flag, but worth noting since it also applies to any stolen refresh token replayed with the header/cookie pair.

User.email has no DB-level uniqueness (Django default); iexact uniqueness is app-level only — a registration/update race could produce duplicate emails making password-reset's .first() lookup ambiguous. Consider a functional unique index on lower(email).
SocialLoginQuery IntegrityError fallback re-queries by email only: a username-collision race (not email) re-raises -> 500. Availability nit.

is_active is not re-checked per request by SimpleJWT JWTAuthentication nor on TokenRefresh — sessions issued before a deactivation stay valid until expiry/blacklist (library behavior; the Google-issuance bypass is reported separately).
uncovered: frontend/src auth store / Pinia session handling beyond http.js (client-side unit scope).

Render (render.yaml) deployment proxy/XFF chain — compose path verified safe (gunicorn unpublished, nginx real_ip terminates spoofed XFF); Render env-specific NUM_TRUSTED_PROXIES correctness is deployment-side.
